extracted.intended_audience: judges, legal practitioners, forensic psychologists, and students of criminal law/criminology
extracted.subtask_description: A manual-style textbook outlining psychological criteria and considerations for taking, evaluating, and interpreting evidence, testimony, and the mental states of judges, witnesses, examinees, and criminals in criminal procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Individualization of Penal Treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Penal or remedial treatment must be adapted to the specific causes of a man’s crime and to the individual affected by those causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat crime analogously to disease: identify specific causes (heredity, physical/moral make-up, temperament, upbringing, environment) and tailor treatment rather than apply indiscriminate, machine-like punishment (e.g., blanket imprisonment or fines). Emphasizes study and comparison of effects of different methods for different kinds of offenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of Causes of Crime
rubrics_metrics.description: To understand and treat crime we must study all possible data that can be causes of crime: heredity, physical and moral make-up, emotional temperament, youth surroundings, present home, and other conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect systematic, multidisciplinary data (anthropology, medicine, psychology, sociology, economics, penology) to diagnose causes in each case; use this diagnosis to choose individualized preventive or remedial measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method (General Considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: The method to be used in taking and evaluating evidence should be scientific and systematic rather than mechanical or ritualistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt methods of natural science where feasible: careful observation, experiment, classification, and hypothesis-testing; avoid uncritical reliance on procedure or form over substantive psychological understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Natural Science in Evidence-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of natural-science methods (empirical observation, controlled comparison) to the study of cases and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use empirical, experimental and comparative procedures in gathering and evaluating testimony and behavior; test hypotheses about causes and reliability rather than assuming legal formalities guarantee truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychologic Lessons (General Considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles from psychology that bear on evidence, testimony, and judicial decision-making must be understood and applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judges and practitioners should be familiar with both theoretical and practical psychological doctrines to interpret perception, memory, inference, emotion, and deception in judicial contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity of Witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: The moral honesty or probity of a witness as a factor in evaluating testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess character-signs, external behavior, and context that bear on a witness’s tendency to tell the truth; integrate with other psychological evidence rather than rely solely on reputation or formality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness of Testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which testimony accurately reflects what actually occurred or was perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate sensory limitations, illusions, memory distortions, inference-vs-observation confusions, emotional influences, and preconceptions when judging correctness; distinguish observation from judgment and inference in testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presuppositions of Evidence-Taking
rubrics_metrics.description: Implicit assumptions and background premises that underlie the collection and interpretation of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of cultural, cognitive, and procedural presuppositions that may bias evidence-gathering; question them and adjust method to reduce systematic error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egoism
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-interest and self-centered motives that influence behavior and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how personal advantage, reputation, or self-protection may shape statements and actions; probe for motives and cross-check with objective data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of concealed facts, private motives, and withheld information in producing or distorting testimony and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect indicators of concealment (hesitation, inconsistency, evasiveness) and seek corroborative evidence; remember that secrets may alter apparent motives and demeanor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of personal, financial, social, or legal interest that may bias witnesses or parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify conflicts of interest, incentives, or stakes (e.g., reward, revenge, promotion) and weigh testimony accordingly; cross-examine and seek independent corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phenomenology: The Outward Expression of Mental States
rubrics_metrics.description: The outward bodily and behavioral signs by which inner mental states are expressed and may be observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study general external conditions, gestures, facial expression, dress, reflexes, and other somatic signs as cues to inner states, but avoid overreliance on single signs; interpret within context and corroborate.

rubrics_metrics.name: General External Conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Environmental and situational factors that influence outward expression and perception (lighting, noise, crowding, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for external conditions when evaluating witness observation and demeanor; poor lighting, distance, or distractions degrade accuracy and alter behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Signs of Character
rubrics_metrics.description: Observable habitual behaviors and mannerisms that indicate underlying character traits relevant to credibility and disposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for consistency of traits across contexts; combine physiognomic, behavioral, and biographical data rather than inferring character from a single gesture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Character-signs
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific observable signs that suggest particular character traits (e.g., nervous tics, bluntness, courtesy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use such signs as part of a broader assessment, noting cultural and individual variation; beware of stereotyping from isolated signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Somatic Character-Units
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical components (posture, facial expression, gestures) that form units from which character inferences may be drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze clusters of somatic signs rather than single indicators; evaluate probable causes (habit, emotion, culture) before drawing moral conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of Irritation
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that provoke physical or emotional irritation which may alter testimony or behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify sources of irritation (pain, fatigue, provocation, environmental discomfort) as potential distorters of perception, memory, and expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cruelty (as a character sign)
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavioral or somatic indicators suggesting cruel disposition or propensity for harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret cruelty signs in context: consider provocation, cultural norms, and whether observed behavior is situational or dispositional; corroborate with history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nostalgia (as a character sign)
rubrics_metrics.description: Longing or sentimental attitudes observable in demeanor that may influence testimony or motive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize nostalgic bias as influencing perception and retrospective accounts; account for idealization or altered memory of past events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflex Movements
rubrics_metrics.description: Involuntary or automatic bodily reactions that can reveal irritation, surprise, or other affects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflexes as rapid, often honest indicators of immediate emotional states, but beware of attributing complex motives to simple reflexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress
rubrics_metrics.description: Clothing and grooming as observable elements that may affect perception of character or social status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of social bias in interpreting dress; dress may influence credibility assessments socially but is not definitive of moral qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physiognomy and Related Subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: The study of facial features and bodily form as purported indicators of character or mental traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat physiognomic inferences cautiously; historical interest in physiognomy exists but modern caution: avoid deterministic judgments and seek corroborating behavioral and biographical data.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Hand
rubrics_metrics.description: The hand (gestures, grip, manual features) as expressive of temperament or character-signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe hands for nervousness, strength, dexterity, or habitual gestures; treat as one cue among many rather than conclusive evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Making of Inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods and pitfalls in inferring causes, intentions, and facts from observed phenomena and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between observation and inference; apply rules of logic, probability, and analogy carefully; be alert to false causal leaps and confirmation bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards and processes by which a proposition is established from evidence and inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify what constitutes adequate proof in context: weigh direct observation, corroboration, motive, and the reliability of sources; consider degrees of certainty rather than absolute proof in many cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Determining cause-and-effect relations in events and behavior relevant to criminal responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully separate correlation from causation; seek evidence of causal mechanisms (psychological, physical, social) and avoid simplistic causal narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: A critical attitude of doubt and testing applied to inferences and testimonial claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain healthy skepticism: test hypotheses, seek disconfirming evidence, and avoid premature certainty; skepticism must be balanced with openness to valid testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Empirical Method in the Study of Cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Using observation, comparison and experiment where possible to study individual cases empirically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect data, compare similar cases, and where feasible apply controlled observation or small-scale experimentation to validate interpretations of behavior and testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Using similarity to known or earlier cases as a basis for inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use analogical reasoning cautiously; check for relevant dissimilarities and avoid overgeneralization from superficial similarities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying probability concepts to weigh the likelihood of competing hypotheses about events or testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess relative probabilities given the evidence; use statistical thinking where available (e.g., base rates) and avoid ignoring low-probability but critical explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition of random, accidental, or chance factors that may explain an event or discrepancy in testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider randomness or coincidence as possible explanations and weigh them against causal accounts; avoid forcing causal narratives when chance is plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persuasion and Explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishing rhetorical persuasion from genuine explanatory argument in testimony and expert statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether statements aim to persuade (rhetoric, emotion, framing) versus explain (causal mechanism, evidence); prefer explanations supported by data over mere persuasive language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference and Judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: The cognitive processes by which observations are turned into judicial judgments and decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of cognitive biases, affective influences, and logical fallacies that can distort inference; cultivate methods for checking and revising initial judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistaken Inferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Common forms and causes of erroneous inferential conclusions in judicial contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify sources of error (overgeneralization, confounding factors, misread signs, unwarranted analogy) and correct via cross-checking, corroboration, and application of methodological safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistics of the Moral Situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of statistical and aggregate data about moral/behavioral phenomena to inform inferences about individual cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ statistics (base rates, distributions) to contextualize individual behavior, but take care in applying group-level data to single-case judgments (ecological fallacy risks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The epistemic status of what is claimed as known in judicial settings—distinction between belief, plausible inference, and secure knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify degrees of certainty for claims, require adequate evidence for assertions presented as knowledge, and distinguish practical/legal standards from scientific certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense Perception (General)
rubrics_metrics.description: The functioning and limitations of human senses as the basis for observing events and producing testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for sensory limits, acuity differences, situational impairment, and the difference between sensation and interpretation when evaluating eyewitness observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of Sight
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual perception specifics relevant to witness observation: acuity, distance, lighting, motion, attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider factors like lighting, distance, angle, movement, color vision, and focus of attention when judging reliability of visual testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color-vision
rubrics_metrics.description: The capacity and limits of color perception and its bearing on accurate descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of color-vision limitations, individual differences (color blindness), and context effects in color reports; corroborate with physical evidence when color is material.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Blind Spot
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiological features of vision (e.g., physiological blind spot) that can produce perceptual gaps or errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize physiological limits that can create unobserved gaps or misperceptions, especially in complex visual scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Sense of Hearing
rubrics_metrics.description: Auditory perception limitations and illusions relevant to witness testimony (distance, masking, selective attention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider ambient noise, hearing acuity, expectancy effects, and misattribution of sounds when assessing auditory reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Sense of Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste perception and its limited role in forensic observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledge taste’s subjectivity and susceptibility to suggestion; treat taste testimony cautiously unless supported by chemical or physical evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Sense of Smell
rubrics_metrics.description: Olfactory perception’s role and limitations in identifying odors, substances, or states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Olfaction is highly subjective and affected by habituation and suggestion; corroborate smell-based claims with physical testing when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Sense of Touch
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactile perception issues relevant to events involving physical contact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for factors like clothing, pressure, numbness, expectation, and suggestibility when relying on touch-based testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception and Conception
rubrics_metrics.description: How raw sensory input is organized into percepts and conceptual understanding; distinction between what is perceived and what is inferred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train to disentangle sensory impressions from conceptual interpretations; watch for conflation of inference with observation in witness accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination
rubrics_metrics.description: Role of imagination in producing or altering recollections, confabulation, and fabricated detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate imaginative reconstruction from veridical memory; be cautious of repeated questioning or suggestion that can inflate imaginative additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual Processes (Mechanism of Thinking, Subconscious, Subjective Conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cognitive mechanics of thinking, including subconscious influences and subjective conditions affecting reasoning and memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider subconscious biases, heuristics, fatigue, stress, and other subjective states when evaluating the reliability of thought processes and testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association of Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: How ideas become linked in memory and thought, affecting recall and inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be alert to associative errors (false linkage), priming effects, and how associative chains can produce plausible but inaccurate recollections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recollection and Memory (Essence)
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature of memory as a reconstructive process rather than a literal recording of past events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess memory as fallible: examine forms of reproduction, distortions, suggestibility, decay, and the influence of later information on recollection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of Reproduction (Memory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different modes by which memories are re-expressed (voluntary recall, spontaneous recollection, recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate reliability differences across modes: recognition may be easier but prone to false positives; spontaneous recall may omit details yet be less contaminated by suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peculiarities of Reproduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual differences and situational factors that alter how memory is reproduced (salience, emotion, rehearsal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how emotion, rehearsal, and importance affect memory fidelity and the likelihood of distortions or perseveration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusions of Memory
rubrics_metrics.description: False memories, confabulations, and distortions that feel subjectively real to the rememberer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use corroboration, timeline checks, and awareness of suggestive interviewing techniques to detect memory illusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mnemotechnique
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques for improving memory and structuring recall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that trained mnemonics can alter recall patterns; trained witnesses or experts may reproduce information differently than untrained witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Will
rubrics_metrics.description: Volitional aspects of behavior and decision-making (intent, choice, compulsion) relevant to criminal responsibility and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish voluntary acts from involuntary or compelled behavior; consider psychological states (coercion, compulsion, impaired volition) in assessing culpability and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotional states and their effects on perception, memory, behavior, and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether emotion is causal or consequential in a situation; strong emotions distort perception and memory, and may produce exaggerated or minimized accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of Giving Testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Different manners and modes by which witnesses express their accounts (narrative, fragmented, dialectal, incorrect forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that cultural, educational, and dialectal differences affect form; interpret expression form sensitively and focus on content reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety in Forms of Expression (including Dialect Forms and Incorrect Forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic and expressive variations that can complicate understanding and assessment of testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful to distinguish genuine inaccuracies due to language or cultural expression from willful deceit; use interpreters and clarifying questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex Differences in Testimony (Women)
rubrics_metrics.description: General differences in perception, expression, and testimony between men and women as treated in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider documented differences (e.g., emotional disposition, particular feminine qualities) but avoid stereotyping; evaluate individuals on their merits and corroborate with objective evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual Peculiarities (Menstruation, Pregnancy, Erotic and Submerged Sexual Factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiological and sexual conditions that may affect behavior, emotion, and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for effects of menstrual cycle, pregnancy, and sexual preoccupation or repression on mood, suggestibility, and demeanor; do not over-attribute testimony content to sexual condition without evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particular Feminine Qualities (Intelligence, Judgment, Honesty, Love/Hate/Friendship, Emotional Disposition, Weakness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes historically discussed as characteristic of women that may influence testimony and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these historical categories as hypotheses to be tested against actual behavior; guard against bias and consider social/cultural influences on expressed traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children as Witnesses / Juvenile Delinquency
rubrics_metrics.description: Special considerations for the testimony and culpability of children and youths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust expectations for memory, understanding, suggestibility, and expressive ability; use child-appropriate interviewing, be cautious of leading questions, consider developmental factors in delinquency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senility
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of aging and senility on perception, memory, judgment, and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cognitive decline, memory impairment, and susceptibility to suggestion; corroborate elderly testimony with independent evidence when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences in Conception (Nature vs. Nurture)
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence of innate disposition and environmental upbringing on perception, behavior, and criminal propensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider both heredity and education/nurture when interpreting behavior; avoid deterministic conclusions based solely on one factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of Nurture, Education, and Inclination
rubrics_metrics.description: How upbringing, level and type of education, and individual inclinations shape testimony, understanding, and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the uneducated’s views, onesided education, and predispositions when assessing comprehension, reliability, and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolated Influences: Habit
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect of habitual behavior patterns on perception/actions and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize habitual responses that may be automatic and not reflect conscious intent; examine history of behavior for habitual patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heredity
rubrics_metrics.description: Genetic and hereditary dispositions that influence temperament, impulse control, and propensity for certain behaviors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heredity as one factor among many; avoid simplistic biological determinism and seek environmental and situational explanations as well.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepossession
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudgment, bias or preconceived notions that distort perception and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect and correct for prepossessions (confirmatory bias) in witnesses, jurors, and judges by exposing contradictory evidence and fostering critical scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation and the Crowd
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of imitation, mob behavior, and social contagion on perception and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of reports from groups where crowd dynamics can produce conformity, shared false memories, or exaggerated accounts; triangulate individual statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passion and Emotion (Isolated Influence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strong passions and emotions as forces that distort motive, perception, and recollection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether emotion is driving testimony or behavior, possibly obscuring objective facts; consider temporality (emotion as cause vs effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor
rubrics_metrics.description: Social reputation, notions of honor, and their influence on testimony and behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider honor-related motives to explain concealment, self-sacrifice, or retaliatory behavior; probe cultural definitions of honor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superstition
rubrics_metrics.description: Superstitious beliefs that may shape perception, explanation of events, and credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for superstitious frameworks in how witnesses explain or interpret events; distinguish belief-based accounts from factual claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mistakes of the Senses: Optical Illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual misperceptions and illusions that lead to erroneous testimony or inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize specific optical phenomena that can mislead (size/distance illusions, motion perception errors); test witness accounts against physical possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Auditory Illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Misperceptions of sounds (source confusion, misheard words) that affect reliability of auditory testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider acoustical conditions and potential for misattribution; corroborate auditory reports when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusions of Touch
rubrics_metrics.description: Tactile misperceptions that can produce erroneous reports about physical contact or sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess circumstances (gloves, clothing, neuropathy) that might cause mistaken tactile reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusions of Taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in gustatory identification or assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat taste-based identifications cautiously and corroborate with chemical/physical tests where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusions of the Olfactory Sense
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in smell perception leading to mistaken identification of odors, substances, or states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Olfactory reports are prone to habituation and suggestion; validate with objective testing if material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hallucinations and Illusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction and forensic significance of hallucinations (percepts without external stimulus) and sensory/cognitive illusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate pathological hallucination from misperception; consider mental health, intoxication, fatigue, and stress as causes; seek psychiatric evaluation when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginative Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Products of imagination that may intrude into testimony as if real memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify imaginative elaboration, confabulation, and influence of suggestion; use timeline, corroboration, and cross-examination to separate imagination from fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misunderstandings (Verbal and Other)
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors arising from linguistic or communicative misunderstandings between parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify ambiguous language, use careful questioning, and consider translation/dialect issues to avoid misconstruing testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Lie (General)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate falsehoods and their psychological forms and motivations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect lying by triangulating inconsistency, motive, and behavior; distinguish lying from pathoformic or psychologically driven falsehoods and from honest errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Pathoformic Lie
rubrics_metrics.description: A pathological form of lying (compulsive or symptomatic) distinct from intentional deceit for gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize compulsive/confabulatory lies rooted in psychological conditions; consider expert psychiatric/psychological assessment rather than punitive presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sleep and Dream (Special Condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of sleep, dreams, and sleep-related phenomena on perception and reported experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of dream reports confused for waking experiences; investigate time, state of consciousness, and possibility of parasomnia or sleep-impaired testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intoxication
rubrics_metrics.description: Effects of alcohol or drugs on perception, memory, volition, and reliability of testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess level and timing of intoxication; recognize impairments to perception and memory and potential for both diminished responsibility and unreliable testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence of suggestion (interviewing, leading questions, social cues) on memory and testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid suggestive questioning; apply neutral, open-ended techniques in interviews; be aware that suggestion can create false memories or alter reports.
